How much cash does a move release? Reconcile both homes and both mortgages

Use four graphics to separate a headline home-price difference from the cash remaining after loans, transaction costs and the replacement purchase.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore the cash available after a move

Interactive planning lab

Cash after selling and repaying old loan$609,000
Cash required for replacement and move$479,500
Cash released / additional cash needed$129,500

Hypothetical sale and replacement purchase settled together. Sale proceeds first pay entered selling costs, other sale-side costs/tax provision and current mortgage. Replacement cash requirement includes price, purchase costs and moving costs less the assumed new mortgage. Percentage costs are placeholders, not statutory tax calculations or quotations. New financing, closing sequence, bridge interest, actual tax liabilities and mortgage approval are not determined. Negative released cash means additional funding is needed.

The central idea

A cheaper replacement home does not automatically release the difference in prices. Mortgage balances, transaction costs and the funding of the replacement determine the cash result.

01

Start with the proceeds available after selling

The sale price is a gross amount. Before assigning it to another goal, account for the current mortgage repayment and the applicable selling costs. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s selling guide lists costs such as legal and discharge fees and possible commissions, moving expenses and mortgage prepayment charges.

This model separates a percentage-based selling allowance from other sale-side costs and a tax provision. The percentages and fixed amounts are hypothetical inputs, not commission quotations, statutory tax rates or a calculation of a mortgage penalty.

The default CAD 900,000 sale less CAD 36,000 of percentage-based costs, CAD 5,000 of other provisions and a CAD 250,000 mortgage repayment leaves CAD 609,000. The model does not determine whether a tax exemption applies or calculate tax due on the sale.

02

Fund the replacement and the move

The next step is the replacement purchase price, its purchase costs, and moving or setup costs, less the assumed new mortgage. The FCAC’s homebuying guide emphasizes upfront costs beyond the mortgage and lists examples of closing expenses.

For a CAD 650,000 replacement, a 3% purchase-cost allowance adds CAD 19,500 and moving costs add CAD 5,000. The default 30% assumed mortgage finances CAD 195,000. The cash needed for those settlements is therefore CAD 479,500.

The assumed mortgage percentage is a scenario input. It does not establish qualification, available proceeds, insurance treatment, interest rates or monthly affordability. A real plan needs confirmed financing and actual closing figures. The tool’s percentage-based cost allowances also cannot replace calculations of charges that follow different rules.

03

Read the full reconciliation

The waterfall adds sale proceeds, subtracts sale costs, repays the old loan, pays for the replacement and its costs, and adds the new financing. Its endpoint is cash released or additional cash needed under the selected assumptions.

The default net cash release is CAD 129,500. The home-price difference alone is CAD 250,000, but mortgage debt falls by CAD 55,000 and entered transaction and moving costs total CAD 65,500. Those uses of funds explain why the price difference overstates the cash available for another goal.

The step order is an accounting reconciliation, not a closing calendar. In particular, adding mortgage funding as a later step does not assert that the borrower must first pay the purchase price entirely in cash. The model assumes the settlements occur together; a different sequence requires a separate timing and bridging review.

04

Separate liquidity from a change in wealth

The home-value and mortgage bars show equity before costs for each property. More new borrowing can increase the cash released while leaving less equity in the replacement. That is a change in the financing mix, rather than a gain created by the move.

The bookkeeping check is replacement home equity + signed cash released = current home equity − transaction and moving costs, within this simplified model. A negative cash-release figure means outside cash is needed, rather than negative money that can be assigned to a goal.

For example, setting the default replacement mortgage to zero creates a CAD 65,500 additional cash requirement, even though the replacement price is lower. The mortgage-free purchase consumes the former equity, and the entered transaction costs still need funding. The debt choice therefore belongs alongside the desired use of the released cash.

05

Test prices, costs and the post-move budget

The cost bars make each allowance visible. The matrix then varies sale and replacement prices around the selected values. The current mortgage and fixed costs remain unchanged, while percentage-based costs and the assumed replacement mortgage scale with the relevant price.

Each signed cell is a cash position, with no probability attached. A positive amount does not establish that the replacement is affordable over time, and a negative amount does not identify a source of additional funding. Consider actual sale conditions, deposit dates, lender funding and settlement costs separately.

The ongoing budget may also change through mortgage payments, property costs, utilities, maintenance, transport or care needs. This tool computes the settlement ledger, not those future expenses or retirement-income adequacy. Review the cash release together with the new obligations before assigning the apparent surplus to spending, saving or another commitment.
